units.name: Case: working a big buy order

terms.short: The full order before it's split up
terms.definition: The whole quantity a fund wants to buy or sell, as handed to the trader or the algo. It's cut into many smaller child orders so it doesn't move the market.
examples: The parent order is 5 lakh shares; the algo will work it through the day.
terms.fill: The fund wants 10 lakh shares of HDFC Bank today. That full quantity is the ____.
wrong: An order placed by a holding company
The first order of the trading day
An order that must fill completely or not at all

terms.short: One small slice of a bigger order
terms.definition: One of the small orders an algo or trader sends to the market to work a larger parent order. Small slices hide the full size and take liquidity a bit at a time.
examples: Each child order was under 2,000 shares, so nobody saw the size.
terms.fill: The algo sends 400 small orders of 2,500 shares each; every one of them is a ____.
wrong: An order placed on a minor's account
An order for a subsidiary's shares
The part of an order that didn't fill

terms.short: Reference price to judge a fill against
terms.definition: The price a trade's average fill is compared with to judge how well it was done, such as the arrival price, VWAP or the close. Which one you pick changes what counts as a good trade.
examples: The PM wants the close as the execution benchmark, so we'll do most of it in the closing auction.
terms.fill: Before we start, agree the ____: are we measured against the arrival price, VWAP or the close?
wrong: Index a fund's returns are compared with
Target price set by an analyst
Price at which the stock last traded

terms.short: Mid price when the order reached the desk
terms.definition: The mid price at the moment an order reaches the trading desk or the algo. Measuring fills against it captures everything that happens once trading starts: spread, impact and drift.
examples: We bought at 1,503 against an arrival price of 1,500, so 20 bp of cost.
terms.fill: The stock's mid was 820 when the order hit the algo, so 820 is the ____.
wrong: Price of the first fill
Closing price of the day before
Price at which the stock first listed

calcs.q: Arrival price is 400.00 and your buy order averages 400.60. What's the cost in basis points?

terms.short: Price when the fund decided to trade
terms.definition: The price when the portfolio manager decided to trade, which can be well before the order reaches the market. Any move between the decision and the order's arrival is delay cost.
examples: The PM decided at 9:20 with the stock at 610, but the order only reached us at 11.
terms.fill: The PM chose to buy when the stock was 610, and the order reached the desk at 615. The 610 is the ____.
wrong: Price an analyst's model says the stock is worth
Price at which a stop-loss triggers
Price set by the exchange at the open

terms.short: Average traded price, weighted by volume
terms.definition: The average price of all trades over a period, each weighted by its size. Buying below the day's VWAP, or selling above it, is a common sign of a good fill, though it says little when your own order is a big part of the volume.
examples: We bought 3 lakh shares at 2 bp better than VWAP.
terms.fill: Add up price × quantity for every trade today, divide by the total quantity, and you get the ____.
wrong: Average of the day's high and low
Simple average of prices taken every minute
Average price of the bids in the book

calcs.q: Two trades print: 100 shares at 10 and 300 shares at 12. What's the VWAP?

tf.s: If your order is half the day's volume, beating VWAP proves you traded well.
tf.why: Your own trades make up much of the VWAP, so you're largely being compared with yourself.

terms.short: Average price over equal time slices
terms.definition: The plain average of prices sampled at equal time intervals, ignoring volume. As a way of trading, it means doing equal amounts in each time slice.
examples: Volume in this stock comes in lumps, so we'll measure against TWAP instead.
terms.fill: Take the price every five minutes from 10 am to 2 pm, ignore how much traded, and average them. That's the ____.
wrong: Average price weighted by trade size
Price at the middle of the trading day
Average of the open and the close

calcs.q: Prices sampled each hour are 100, 102, 101 and 105. What's the TWAP?

terms.short: Paper return minus the real return of a trade
terms.definition: The gap between what a trade would have made if it had filled at the decision price with no costs, and what it really made. It adds up delay, spread, impact, fees and the cost of shares that never filled.
examples: Implementation shortfall on the rebalance was 35 bp, most of it from chasing in the last hour.
terms.fill: On paper the fund bought at 500 with no costs; in reality it paid 503 plus fees. That gap is the ____.
wrong: Margin shortfall at the end of the day
Shares delivered short in settlement
Gap between the target price and the current price

calcs.q: The decision price was 500. You bought 1,000 shares at an average of 503, with no fees. What's the shortfall in basis points?
calcs.why: 3 ÷ 500 = 0.6%, which is 60 bp, or ₹3,000 on the order.

tf.s: Shares you meant to buy but never filled add nothing to implementation shortfall.
tf.why: If the price ran away, the gain you missed counts as opportunity cost.

terms.short: Your share of the market's volume
terms.definition: Your trades as a share of all the volume traded while you work the order. The higher it is, the more you move the price, so desks often cap it at around 10 to 20%.
examples: Keep participation under 10%; this name can't take more.
terms.fill: 500,000 shares traded while you were working and 50,000 were yours, so your ____ was 10%.
wrong: Share of a company owned by the promoter
Share of trades done by retail investors
Weight of one stock in the index

calcs.q: While your algo ran, the stock traded 8 lakh shares, of which 1.2 lakh were yours. What was your participation rate?

terms.short: Fees you can see on the contract note
terms.definition: Trading costs that are billed and shown on the contract note: brokerage, STT, exchange charges, SEBI fees, stamp duty and GST. You know them before you trade, unlike spread and impact.
examples: Explicit costs are 3 bp a side; the impact is ten times that.
terms.fill: Brokerage, STT, exchange charges, stamp duty and GST, all printed on the contract note, are ____.
wrong: Costs from the spread and your own price impact
Tax on the profit from a trade
Interest on borrowed margin

terms.short: Costs hidden in the prices you get
terms.definition: Trading costs that never appear on a bill but show up in your fill prices: the spread, market impact, delay and missed trades. For large orders they usually dwarf the explicit costs.
examples: The broker is cheap on commission, but its implicit costs are awful.
terms.fill: Nobody bills you for the spread or your own price impact, but you pay for them through worse fills. They're ____.
wrong: Fees printed on the contract note
Yearly charge for a demat account
Tax deducted at source on dividends

terms.short: Algo that works an order at low cost
terms.definition: An algorithm whose only job is to buy or sell a given quantity cheaply, by deciding when, where and how big to make each slice. It doesn't choose what to trade; the portfolio manager or the strategy has already done that.
examples: Hand the order to an execution algo and check on it at lunch.
terms.fill: The PM picks the stock; the ____ decides how to slice and time the buying so it costs as little as possible.
wrong: Algo that decides which stocks to buy
Rule that fires a stop-loss order
Software that settles trades after the close

tf.s: An execution algo decides whether a trade is worth doing.
tf.why: It only decides how to carry out a trade someone else has chosen.

terms.short: Trades in step with the usual volume pattern
terms.definition: An execution algo that spreads an order across the day in line with the stock's usual volume profile, aiming to finish close to the day's VWAP. It's predictable, which makes it easier for others to spot.
examples: Put half on a VWAP algo to the close and keep half for the auction.
terms.fill: If 20% of a stock's volume usually trades in the first hour, this algo plans to do 20% of your order then. It's a ____.
wrong: Trades the same amount every few minutes
Trades a fixed share of live volume
Trades as fast as it can at the open

terms.short: Trades equal amounts at even intervals
terms.definition: An execution algo that cuts an order into equal slices sent at regular times, whatever the volume. It's simple and suits thin stocks or a fixed window, but it trades the same amount in quiet and busy spells.
examples: TWAP algo, 2,000 shares every five minutes until 2 pm.
terms.fill: Buying 1,000 shares every 10 minutes from open to close, however busy the stock is, is what a ____ does.
wrong: Trades in step with the usual volume pattern
Trades a fixed share of live volume
Trades only when the price dips

terms.short: Trades a fixed share of live volume
terms.definition: An execution algo that keeps your trades at a set percentage of the market's live volume, such as 10%. It speeds up when the stock is busy and slows when it's quiet, so you don't know in advance when it will finish.
examples: Run it POV at 8%; if volume dries up, we'll carry the rest to tomorrow.
terms.fill: Set it to 10% and it buys 1,000 shares for every 10,000 the market trades. It's a ____.
wrong: Trades equal amounts at even intervals
Trades in step with yesterday's volume
Fills the whole order in one go

calcs.q: You need 2 lakh shares on a POV algo at 10%. The stock trades about 40 lakh shares a day. How much market volume must trade for you to finish?
options: A tenth of a day's volume
calcs.why: 2 lakh at 10% needs 20 lakh shares of market volume, which is half of 40 lakh.

tf.s: A POV algo always finishes by the end of the day.
tf.why: If volume is light, it can run out of day with shares left to do.

terms.short: Trades early to stay close to arrival price
terms.definition: An execution algo that aims to keep implementation shortfall against the arrival price low. It trades harder at the start, accepting more impact to cut the risk that the price drifts away while it waits.
examples: The news is out, so use the arrival price algo and get most of it done this hour.
terms.fill: News is breaking, so you want an algo that front-loads the order to finish near where the price was when you started. You pick an ____.
wrong: Trades equal amounts at even intervals
Waits for the closing auction
Trades in step with the usual volume pattern

terms.short: How a stock's volume spreads through the day
terms.definition: The usual pattern of how much of a stock's daily volume trades in each part of the day, built from past days. In most stock markets it's U-shaped: heavy at the open and the close, lighter in the middle.
examples: Our volume profile says a quarter of the day trades in the last 45 minutes.
terms.fill: A VWAP algo plans its slices from the stock's ____, which shows heavy trading at the open and close.
wrong: Chart of price against time
List of a stock's biggest holders
Number of shares waiting in the order book

terms.short: How hard an algo trades against the clock
terms.definition: An algo setting for how fast to get the order done. High urgency crosses the spread and takes liquidity, paying more impact; low urgency waits with passive orders, risking that the price moves away.
examples: Turn up the urgency, the stock's starting to run.
terms.fill: Turn the ____ up and the algo crosses the spread more often to finish sooner, paying more impact.
wrong: How soon a trade must settle
Priority the exchange gives to large orders
How quickly an order can be cancelled

terms.short: Client orders going straight to the exchange
terms.definition: A broker facility that lets clients send orders straight into the exchange's trading system through the broker's systems, without a dealer keying them in. The broker's risk checks still apply. SEBI allowed it for institutional clients in April 2008.
examples: The fund uses DMA, so its own algos send orders to NSE through our gateway.
terms.fill: The fund's traders enter orders on their own screens and they go straight into NSE through the broker's systems, with nobody at the broker re-keying them. That's ____.
wrong: A demat account held directly with NSDL
Buying shares straight from the company
Trading without paying any brokerage

tf.s: With DMA, the broker's risk checks are skipped.
tf.why: Orders still pass through the broker's systems and risk controls.

terms.short: Review of what trades really cost
terms.definition: Measuring what trades really cost against benchmarks such as the arrival price or VWAP, split into fees, spread, impact and delay. Done before trading, it estimates the cost; done afterwards, it checks what really happened.
examples: Post-trade TCA shows the afternoon orders cost twice as much as the morning ones.
terms.fill: Each quarter the fund checks every fill against arrival price and VWAP to see which brokers and algos cost most. That's ____.
wrong: Tax collected on each trade
Software that sends orders to the exchange
SEBI's audit of a broker's accounts

terms.short: The price move your own trading causes
terms.definition: How far your own buying or selling pushes the price over the whole life of an order. Unlike impact cost, which is read off the order book for one instant sweep, it includes how other traders react while you keep trading.
examples: The spread was 2 bp, but market impact on the full order was 25 bp.
terms.fill: As you kept buying all morning, the stock climbed 1% on your own demand. That move is ____.
wrong: How news about a company moves its stock
How the index moves when one stock moves
Effect of an earnings beat on the share price

tf.s: Doubling an order's size roughly doubles its market impact per share.
tf.why: Impact grows more slowly than size, roughly with its square root.

terms.short: Price push that fades once you stop
terms.definition: The part of your market impact that comes from using up the liquidity on offer. It fades once you stop trading and the order book refills.
examples: Half the move was temporary impact; the stock gave it back within the hour.
terms.fill: Part of your price push comes only from eating the offers in the book, and it fades as the book refills. That part is ____.
wrong: Price move that stays after you stop
Price move caused by a news headline
Gap between the open and the previous close

terms.short: Price move that stays after you stop
terms.definition: The part of your market impact that stays after you finish, because other traders read your buying or selling as news about what the stock is worth.
examples: There's a big buyer in the name, so most of that move is permanent impact.
terms.fill: Others guessed a big fund was buying and repriced the stock, so the 15 bp move never came back. That's ____.
wrong: Price push that fades once you stop
Change in price after a stock split
Fall in price on the ex-dividend date

terms.short: Impact grows with the square root of size
terms.definition: A pattern found across many markets: the market impact of an order grows with the square root of its size relative to daily volume, scaled by the stock's volatility. Four times the size costs about twice as much per share, not four times.
examples: By the square-root law, cutting the order to a quarter should halve the impact.
terms.fill: Impact per share grows with √(order size ÷ daily volume), a pattern known as the ____.
wrong: Volatility grows with the square root of time
Impact grows in a straight line with order size
Returns fall as the square of fund size
terms.note: σ is daily volatility, Q the order size, V daily volume and Y a constant close to 1.

calcs.q: An order of 1% of daily volume costs about 10 bp of impact. Using the square-root law, what does an order of 4% of daily volume cost?
calcs.why: 4 times the size gives √4 = 2 times the impact: 2 × 10 = 20 bp.

terms.short: Price drift before the order reaches market
terms.definition: The cost of the price moving between the portfolio manager's decision and the order reaching the market. It's part of implementation shortfall, and often nobody on the desk owns it.
examples: The order sat in the PM's inbox for an hour and lost 15 bp before we touched it.
terms.fill: The PM decided to buy at 200, but by the time the order reached the desk the stock was 202. Those 2 rupees are ____.
wrong: Penalty for paying margin late
Interest charged when settlement is late
Cost of an order left unfilled at the close

terms.short: Gain missed on shares that never filled
terms.definition: In execution, the gain you missed on shares you meant to trade but didn't, because the price ran away or your limit was too tight. In everyday finance it means what you give up by choosing one use of money over another.
examples: Our limit was too tight: we got half the order, and the opportunity cost on the rest was bigger than any impact.
terms.fill: You bought 60% of the order, then the stock ran 5% and you gave up on the rest. The gain missed on the other 40% is ____.
wrong: Brokerage charged on a cancelled order
Price paid above the arrival price
Interest earned on idle cash

calcs.q: You decided to buy 10,000 shares at 100 but filled only 6,000. The stock ends at 110. What's the opportunity cost on the unfilled part?

terms.short: Risk the price moves while you trade slowly
terms.definition: The risk that the price moves against you while an order is worked slowly. Trading faster cuts timing risk but raises impact, and balancing the two is the core problem of execution.
examples: Spreading it over three days cuts impact but piles on timing risk.
terms.fill: Working the order over a week keeps impact low, but leaves you exposed to the price wandering off. That exposure is ____.
wrong: Risk that the exchange opens late
Risk of buying at the day's high
Risk that settlement takes longer than T+1

terms.short: Others spotting your order before it's done
terms.definition: When other traders work out that a big order is in the market, from its pattern of child orders or from loose talk, and trade ahead of it. It raises the cost of finishing the order.
examples: The same size every 30 seconds is a giveaway; that's where the information leakage started.
terms.fill: Your algo sent identical slices every minute, other traders spotted the pattern and bought ahead of you. That's ____.
wrong: Delay in exchange data reaching your screen
A data breach at a stock exchange
Publishing a research report before the open

terms.short: Price drifting back after you finish
terms.definition: How far the price moves back after your order finishes. A big reversion means much of your impact was temporary, which suggests you traded faster or more aggressively than you needed to.
examples: Reversion was 15 bp within 30 minutes; we paid up for liquidity we didn't need.
terms.fill: You finished buying at 505, and twenty minutes later the stock was back at 502. That drop back is ____.
wrong: A stock's bounce after a sharp fall
Reversing a trade booked by mistake
Return of margin after a position is closed

terms.short: Model for the best pace to work an order
terms.definition: The classic model for choosing how fast to work an order. It finds the schedule with the best balance between market impact (from trading fast) and timing risk (from trading slowly) for a given appetite for risk. Many implementation shortfall algos build on it.
examples: With high risk aversion, Almgren–Chriss front-loads the schedule.
terms.fill: The classic model that trades market impact off against timing risk to set an order's schedule is the ____.
wrong: Model for pricing European options
Model that splits returns into factors
Model of how volatility changes over time

terms.short: Share of the order filled so far
terms.definition: How much of an order has been executed, as a share of the total. Sales traders update clients through the day: '40% done at 1,212 against VWAP at 1,214.'
examples: We're 60% done at an average of 2,431, just inside VWAP.
The client wants an update: what's the percent done on the Reliance sell?
terms.fill: By noon 2 lakh of the 5 lakh shares were bought, and the trader told the client the ____ was 40%.
wrong: Share of the day's volume you traded
Share of trades that made money
Share of the price paid upfront

calcs.q: The order is to sell 8 lakh shares. So far 3.2 lakh have been sold. What is the percent done?

terms.short: A big resting order holding the price back
terms.definition: A large order sitting at the best price that stops it moving: a big seller leaning on the offer caps the rise, and a big buyer leaning on the bid props the price up.
examples: Someone's leaning on the offer at 1,450 with 2 lakh shares; we're not getting above it today.
There's a buyer leaning on the bid, so I'd sell into it while it's there.
terms.fill: A seller with 3 lakh shares has sat at ₹820 all morning, so the stock can't get past it: he's ____.
wrong: Waiting for the price to fall to buy
Trading on credit from the broker
Copying another trader's orders

terms.short: Rest a buy at the best bid, in the queue
terms.definition: Placing a passive buy order at the current best bid price, behind the orders already there. It avoids paying the spread, but you wait your turn in the queue and may not get filled.
examples: No rush, join the bid at 612 and see what comes.
Join the offer with half and work the rest through the afternoon.
terms.fill: The best bid was ₹612. Instead of paying ₹612.50, she placed her buy at ₹612 to ____ and wait.
wrong: Buy straight away at the best offer
Sell to the highest bidder right now
Bid one tick above the current best bid

terms.short: Bid a tick higher to go first in line
terms.definition: Placing a buy order one tick above the current best bid, so you become the new best bid and are first to be filled. You pay a little more but jump the queue.
examples: Improve the bid by a tick; there are 50,000 shares ahead of us at 612.
If the offer side's thin, improve the offer and you'll probably get hit.
terms.fill: The best bid had a long queue, so he bid one tick higher to ____ and get filled first.
wrong: Raise the bid to the offer and buy
Rest a buy at the current best bid
Cancel the bid and place it lower

terms.short: Pay the other side's price to trade now
terms.definition: To buy at the offer or sell at the bid, trading straight away against resting orders. You get the fill but pay the spread; a market order or an aggressive limit order crosses it.
examples: We're behind the stock; cross the spread for the next 20,000.
Crossing the spread on every child order cost us 6 bps on the day.
terms.fill: Bid ₹100, offer ₹100.10: buying right away at ₹100.10 means you ____ and pay 10 paise.
wrong: Place your order inside the spread
Wait at the bid for a seller
Trade the gap between two futures

terms.short: Accept a worse price to get it done
terms.definition: To accept a higher price when buying (or a lower one when selling) than you wanted, because getting the trade done matters more. Desks pay up when the stock is running away or news is coming.
examples: It's running away from us; pay up to 1,520 and finish the order.
We had to pay up 30 bps over arrival to get the block.
terms.fill: With results tomorrow and half the order left, the PM told the trader to ____ and finish it, even 1% above arrival.
wrong: Settle the trade with the clearing house
Pay the broker's bill at month end
Pay a margin call in cash

terms.short: Price moving fast away from your order
terms.definition: When the price moves quickly away from where you're trying to trade: up when you're buying, down when you're selling. You either pay up and chase it or risk not getting the order done.
examples: It's running away: up 2% since we started and we're only 30% done.
Don't chase it if it's running away; the client's limit is 1,480.
terms.fill: She was buying slowly at ₹500, but the price jumped to ₹515 in ten minutes; it was ____ from her.
wrong: A trader leaving the firm with clients
Price stuck in a tight range all day
Stock suspended from trading for news

terms.short: A real other side wanting the opposite trade
terms.definition: A buyer or seller who genuinely wants the other side of your trade for their own reasons, not a market maker or an arbitrageur. Finding a natural lets a block trade at a fair price with little impact.
examples: We have a natural for 5 lakh shares: a fund wants to sell exactly what our client is buying.
No natural on the other side, so we'll have to work it in the market.
terms.fill: A pension fund wanted to sell the 3 lakh shares the client wanted to buy, so the broker matched them: it had found a ____.
wrong: A stock that has no futures or options
A trade done with no brokerage at all
A buyer who uses only market orders

terms.short: One chunk of size traded at once
terms.definition: A single piece of size: a slice of a bigger order, or the size of one trade. 'Sell it in 25,000-share clips' means in pieces of that size; 'a ₹50 crore clip' is one big block.
examples: Work it in 10,000-share clips so we don't spook the book.
There's a buyer for a ₹100 crore clip if we can price it.
terms.fill: Instead of one big order, he sold one 20,000-share ____ every few minutes.
wrong: Short video of the trading screen
Fee cut from each trade
Price limit on a single order

terms.short: A sign a firm may trade a block
terms.definition: Short for indication of interest: a message from a broker that it has, or may have, interest in buying or selling a stock in size. It isn't a firm order, so the size and price still have to be agreed.
examples: We're seeing IOIs on the buy side in Infosys; that might be a natural for our seller.
That IOI was stale; the buyer had finished by the time we called.
terms.fill: The broker sent word that a client might buy 10 lakh shares, though nothing was firm yet: an ____.
wrong: A firm order that must be filled
A daily report of open interest
An order sent to the opening auction

terms.short: Patient: price matters more than speed
terms.definition: A client or PM telling the trader to work the order patiently, trading passively and only when the price is good. It lowers impact and spread costs but risks the price drifting away before the order is done.
examples: No rush on the sell; just stay inside VWAP and finish by Friday.
No hurry, but if it breaks 1,400 I want to be done.
terms.fill: The PM said there was ____, so the trader rested small bids all day and finished the order in three days.
wrong: Finish the whole order at once
Cancel the order before the close
Trade only in the closing auction

terms.short: Do more of the order early
terms.definition: To execute more of an order early in the trading window than an even schedule would, for example half in the first hour. It cuts the risk of the price drifting away, at the cost of more impact up front.
examples: Results are tomorrow, so front-load it: half done by lunch.
The algo front-loaded the buy, then slowed down when the spread widened.
terms.fill: Expecting the price to rise during the day, the trader bought 60% of the order in the first hour: she chose to ____ it.
wrong: Leave most of the order for the close
Spread the order evenly over the day
Enter the order into the system early

terms.short: The part of an order still not done
terms.definition: What's left of an order after the fills so far. Near the close traders ask what to do with the residual: finish it, carry it to tomorrow or cancel it.
examples: We've done 7 lakh of 10; what do you want to do with the residual?
Put the residual in the close.
terms.fill: With 8 lakh of the 10 lakh shares bought by 3 pm, the trader asked the PM what to do with the ____.
wrong: The broker's fee after rebates
Fee left to pay after a trade
Cash left in the account at day end

terms.short: Done at the official closing price
terms.definition: Executed at or very near the day's official closing price, which index funds and many PMs use as their benchmark. On NSE that means joining the closing auction for stocks that have one, or trading in the minutes that set the close.
examples: The index fund needs it all done in the close, so we'll put it into the closing auction.
Do half over the day and the rest at the close.
terms.fill: Index funds buying a new member want the whole order done ____, at the official closing price.
wrong: Done in the first minutes of trading
Done at the day's average price
Done after the market has shut

terms.short: Trader may choose price and timing
terms.definition: An order the client gives with discretion: the trader can choose when and at what price to trade, and isn't held to any particular fill. The opposite is a held order, which must be executed straight away.
examples: It's not held, so I'll wait for the opening swings to settle before I start.
The client gave us 5 lakh not held, with a limit of 1,250.
terms.fill: Because the order was ____, the broker waited for the spread to tighten instead of buying at once.
wrong: Order the exchange has rejected
Order held back until the next day
Order with no shares in the account

terms.short: Cancel the live order now
terms.definition: To cancel a working order straight away, often because news has hit or the price has moved. 'Pull the bid' and 'pull the offer' mean cancel your resting buy or sell.
examples: News out on the stock: pull the order until we know what it is.
They pulled the offer the moment we lifted the first 10,000.
terms.fill: The headline flashed and the trader cancelled her resting buy within a second: she had to ____.
wrong: Send the order to another exchange
Raise the order's price to fill it
Book the order in the back office

terms.short: Change price or size of a live order
terms.definition: To change the price or quantity of an order that is still working, instead of cancelling and sending a new one. A price change or a bigger size usually sends the order to the back of the queue.
examples: Amend the order down to 50,000; the client's cut the size.
Amend the limit to 1,420 and keep working.
terms.fill: Instead of cancelling, she changed her bid from ₹612 to ₹614: she chose to ____.
wrong: Cancel the order and start again
Add a stop-loss after the fill
Reverse a trade that has settled

terms.short: Stop for today; finish the rest later
terms.definition: An order instruction or update meaning trading stops for today, usually with the residual carried to the next session or cancelled. A trader who has hit a loss limit or a target says it too.
examples: We're 70% done; done for the day, start again at the open.
Hit my target by noon, so I'm done for the day.
terms.fill: With the stock up 3% and 60% of the order filled, the client said to stop until tomorrow: the order was ____.
wrong: Order fully filled for the client
Order valid only for a day
Trade that settles the same day

terms.short: Cost in basis points against arrival
terms.definition: How an execution is scored: the average fill price compared with the price when the order arrived, in basis points. For a buy, filling above arrival is a cost and below it a gain.
examples: We bought at 1,002 against arrival at 1,000: 20 bips versus arrival.
The algo was 8 bps worse than arrival but 2 bps better than VWAP.
terms.fill: Arrival price ₹500, average buy price ₹501: the desk reports the cost as 20 ____.
wrong: Spread between bid and offer in paise
Cost against the day's closing price
Brokerage as a share of the trade

calcs.q: You sell at an average of ₹995. The arrival price was ₹1,000. What is the cost in bips versus arrival?
calcs.why: You sold ₹5 below arrival. 5 ÷ 1,000 = 0.5%, which is 50 bps of cost.

terms.short: Size-weighted price of all the fills
terms.definition: The price of all the fills on an order, weighted by how many shares each fill was. It is what the client pays or receives, and what gets compared with benchmarks like VWAP and arrival.
examples: Average price on the buy is 2,431.40 against a VWAP of 2,433.
Send the client the average price and the percent done every hour.
terms.fill: Buying 3,000 shares at ₹100 and 1,000 at ₹104 gives an ____ of ₹101.
wrong: Middle of the day's high and low
Average of the bid and the offer
The market's average price for the day

terms.short: Most of the market's volume you'll take
terms.definition: A cap on the share of market volume an order or algo may trade, such as 'no more than 15% of volume'. It limits impact and keeps the order from standing out, but can leave it unfinished on a quiet day.
examples: Max participation 10%, and don't go below 1,200.
On a light day the 15% cap meant we finished only 70% of the order.
terms.fill: The algo was told never to trade more than 20% of the stock's volume: a ____ of 20%.
wrong: Most shares one client may hold
Largest order an exchange allows
Most brokers that may handle an order

terms.short: Record the trade's details for booking
terms.definition: To record a done trade with its details (stock, side, quantity, price, client and time) so it can be booked and settled. It's mostly electronic now, but the phrase has stuck.
examples: Done 2 lakh at 845; write the ticket and send it to the client.
Write the ticket before you take the next call, or the allocations get muddled.
terms.fill: Once the block was agreed at ₹845, the sales trader had to ____ so operations could book it.
wrong: Report a trader to compliance
Write the research note on a stock
Fine a client for a late payment

terms.short: Splitting a block's fills across accounts
terms.definition: Dividing one executed order among the funds or clients it was done for, at the same average price. Fair allocation rules stop a manager from giving the best fills to favoured accounts.
examples: Allocation on the 5 lakh: 3 lakh to fund A and 2 lakh to fund B, all at the average price.
Allocations for today's trades are due before 4 pm.
terms.fill: The manager bought 10 lakh shares in one order and then split them between three schemes at the same price: the ____.
wrong: Brokerage shared between two brokers
Weight of a stock in the Nifty index
Margin limit given to each trader

terms.short: Trade gradually from open to close
terms.definition: An instruction to spread an order across the whole session, usually following the volume curve, instead of doing it at once. It's the natural way to aim for the day's VWAP.
examples: No rush: work it over the day, VWAP benchmark.
Spreading it over the day cut the impact, but the stock drifted up 1% while we bought.
terms.fill: The PM wanted the day's VWAP, so the trader worked the 4 lakh shares ____, in line with the volume curve.
wrong: Done in one trade at the open
Valid until the next session
Held overnight to the next day
